name: Palazzo Pubblico
region: Piazza della Libertà, City of San Marino, Republic of San Marino
architectural_style: Neo-Gothic public palace built 1884–1894 on the site of the medieval original; designed by Francesco Azzurri; Istrian limestone facade with arched windows, crenellated parapet, and clock tower; the building houses the Council Chamber of the Grand and General Council (San Marino's parliament) and the state apartments of the Captains Regent

tagline: The seat of Europe's oldest republic — where the twin Captains Regent govern San Marino from a 19th-century neo-Gothic palace on a square that the world's only surviving medieval-era republic built for exactly this purpose
highlights: The Captains Regent — San Marino's twin heads of state are elected by the Grand Council every six months, one from the majority, one from the minority, and serve simultaneously with mutual veto power; the office has been in continuous operation since 1243, making it one of the oldest continuously functioning executive offices in the world

Open when Parliament isn't in session — Palazzo Pubblico is a working seat of government, not a converted heritage building; it closes when the Grand and General Council sits, during state ceremonies, and at the twice-yearly investiture of the Captains Regent (April 1 and October 1 each year). When open, visitors can tour the Council Chamber and the state rooms

The changing of the guard — the Piazza della Libertà hosts a scheduled ceremonial changing of the guard with the Corpo dei Gendarmi and the Guardie di Rocca in full 15th-century-inspired uniform; one of the few remaining monarchical-style ceremonies in a republic

The State Museums Pass — Palazzo Pubblico access is covered by the same pass as Cesta Tower, Guaita Tower, and four other San Marino sites; the GYG guided tour (t1035756, from €45, 4.9★ / 31 reviews) bundles the pass for all participants

Piazza della Libertà — the 1876 Statue of Liberty (predating the New York version by a decade) stands in the centre of the square facing the palace; the piazza is the social and ceremonial heart of the world's smallest republic by population
description:
The Republic of San Marino makes an unusual claim among the world's nations: it describes itself as the world's oldest surviving republic, with a founding tradition that attributes its origin to a Christian stonecutter named Marinus (later Saint Marinus) who settled on Mount Titano in 301 AD and established a community of fellow Christians there. The documentary evidence for continuous self-governance is more recent — the Statutes of 1263 are the earliest surviving legal text — but the claim to an uninterrupted republican tradition since the medieval period is credible enough that it has never been seriously contested, and San Marino managed to remain independent through the surrounding centuries of Italian warfare, papal politics, Napoleonic reorganisation, and Risorgimento unification.

Palazzo Pubblico is the building from which San Marino has been governed since 1894. The original medieval government palace on this site in Piazza della Libertà was demolished and replaced with the current neo-Gothic building — designed by Roman architect Francesco Azzurri in Istrian limestone, with crenellated parapet, arched windows, and a clock tower — as part of a late 19th-century building programme that gave the city's administrative centre its current character. The building functions as a genuine seat of government: the Grand and General Council (San Marino's parliament) meets in the Council Chamber inside, the Captains Regent use the state rooms for official business, and state ceremonies are conducted on the piazza outside.

This dual function — heritage site and operational government building — produces the central caveat about visiting Palazzo Pubblico: it is **not guaranteed open**. The palace closes for Grand Council sessions, state ceremonies, and the formal investiture of the Captains Regent that takes place twice each year on April 1 and October 1. The GYG guided tour (t1035756) includes Palazzo Pubblico access via the State Museums Pass but explicitly notes this 'when open' condition in its own product description — visitors on the tour can access the palace when it is available, but cannot be guaranteed entry if a state function coincides with their visit.

When open, visitors can see the Council Chamber where San Marino's parliament meets, the formal state rooms used by the Captains Regent, and the building's interior neo-Gothic decoration. The piazza outside is worth time in itself: the 1876 Statue of Liberty — a gilded female figure predating Bartholdi's New York installation by a decade — stands at the centre of the square facing the palace, and the scheduled changing of the guard ceremony brings uniformed troops in 15th-century-style dress to the palace steps.
history: San Marino's governing institutions claim continuity from the medieval period, with the Captains Regent documented since 1243 and the Statutes of 1263 as the earliest surviving legal code. A government building on the Piazza della Libertà site predates the current structure; the medieval palazzo served as the seat of the Grand and General Council for several centuries before being demolished in the 1880s. The current Palazzo Pubblico was built between 1884 and 1894 to designs by Francesco Azzurri, incorporating neo-Gothic architectural vocabulary consistent with the Romantic-era historicism fashionable across Europe in the late 19th century — the same impulse that produced the Hungarian Parliament, the Palace of Westminster's rebuilt sections, and dozens of municipal buildings across Europe. San Marino's historic centre and Mount Titano, including Palazzo Pubblico, were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008.
how_to_visit:
**Getting there:** Palazzo Pubblico is in the centre of San Marino City, on Piazza della Libertà — the main square, immediately accessible from the city gate. From the parking areas on the lower slopes, the walk to the piazza takes 10–15 minutes. Buses from Rimini (Bonelli line, ~45 minutes) arrive near the city gate. By car from Rimini, ~30 minutes via the SP258.

**Tickets:** Entry is covered by the State Museums Pass (~€5 per adult), which also covers Cesta Tower, Guaita Tower, and four other San Marino sites. The GYG small-group guided tour (t1035756, from €45 per person, 4.9★ / 31 reviews) bundles the pass into the tour price. Note: Palazzo Pubblico is only accessible when government functions permit — it closes during Grand Council sessions, state ceremonies, and the Captains Regent investiture on April 1 and October 1 each year. Confirm current accessibility on the day of your visit.

**Practical tips:** Check the official schedule of Grand Council sessions before visiting if Palazzo Pubblico is a priority — sessions are announced in advance on San Marino government channels. The changing of the guard at the palace steps is a scheduled ceremony worth timing your visit around; current schedules are posted at the city's tourist information office near the gate. Even when the palace interior is closed, the piazza, the Statue of Liberty, and the palace facade are freely accessible and make the square worth visiting regardless.

**Combine with:** [Guaita Tower](/castles/san-marino/guaita-tower) (the iconic First Tower on Mount Titano's ridge — the most-photographed structure in San Marino, reached in 20 minutes from the piazza along the fortification walkway) and [Cesta Tower](/castles/san-marino/cesta-tower) (the Second Tower on the highest peak, housing the Museum of Ancient Weapons — covered by the same State Museums Pass).

faqs.question: What are the Captains Regent and why does San Marino have two heads of state?
faqs.answer: The Captains Regent (Capitani Reggenti) are San Marino's twin heads of state — two citizens elected simultaneously by the Grand and General Council (parliament) to serve 6-month terms, one from the parliamentary majority and one from the minority, each holding mutual veto power over the other. The system is designed to prevent the concentration of executive power in a single individual, an arrangement that San Marino's political tradition traces to its medieval republican foundations. The Captains Regent cannot be re-elected for three years after serving a term. The investiture ceremony on April 1 and October 1 each year involves the formal transfer of power in a ceremony at Palazzo Pubblico, and on these days the palace is unavailable for public visiting.

faqs.question: Why does San Marino have a Statue of Liberty that predates the New York one?
faqs.answer: The San Marino Statue of Liberty in Piazza della Libertà was installed in 1876 — ten years before the Bartholdi/Eiffel installation was unveiled in New York Harbour in 1886. The San Marino statue depicts a gilded female figure holding a staff, symbolising the republic's long independence. The coincidence of both statues representing liberty through a female personification reflects the common 19th-century iconographic tradition rather than any direct connection between the two works. San Marino's version is smaller and less famous, but its earlier installation date is a genuine point of local pride.

faqs.question: Is San Marino genuinely the world's oldest republic?
faqs.answer: San Marino's claim to be the world's oldest republic rests on its founding tradition attributing the community's origin to 301 AD and its documentary evidence of continuous self-governance from the 13th century. The Statutes of 1263 are the earliest surviving legal text establishing the republic's constitutional framework. No other currently existing republic can demonstrate an equally long continuous republican tradition with comparable documentary evidence — Venice, Genoa, and other medieval Italian republics no longer exist as independent states. Whether 'oldest republic' requires continuous statehood, continuous constitutional framework, or simply continuous self-governance is a matter of definition, but San Marino's claim on any of these grounds is more credible than any competitor.
